questions.text: How does a reference differ from an ordinary pointer in the explanation?

answers.text: It is guaranteed to point to a valid value of a particular type for the lifetime of the reference
It is always null
It necessarily owns the data
It can exist only for `String`

questions.text: What happens if a function receives `&String` and tries to call `push_str` through that reference?

answers.text: The code does not compile because an immutable reference does not permit mutation
The string is modified
The string is automatically cloned
The reference automatically becomes `&mut String`

questions.explanation: Like variables, references are immutable by default; a `String` cannot be modified through `&String`.

questions.text: Which reference type is needed by a function that must modify a passed `String`?

answers.text: &String
&mut String
String::ref
mut String without `&` is always required

questions.explanation: A mutable reference `&mut String` is used to modify a borrowed value.

questions.text: Why does `let r1 = &mut s; let r2 = &mut s; println!("{r1}, {r2}");` not compile?

answers.text: Two active mutable references to the same value cannot exist at the same time
`String` cannot be declared `mut`
`println!` forbids references
`&mut` works only with numbers

questions.explanation: A mutable reference is exclusive: the second mutable borrow conflicts with the first while the first is still used.

questions.text: What is forbidden while immutable references `r1` and `r2` to `s` are active?

answers.text: Creating `&mut s` if the immutable references will still be used
Creating a second immutable reference
Reading through `r1`
Ending the scope

questions.explanation: You cannot have an active immutable borrow and a mutable borrow of the same data at the same time.

questions.text: When does an immutable borrow stop preventing creation of a mutable reference in the same lexical scope?

answers.text: After the immutable reference's last use, provided the borrows no longer overlap
Only at the closing brace of the current block
Immediately after the reference is created, even if it will be used later
Only after explicitly calling `drop` on the original owner

questions.explanation: With non-lexical lifetimes, a borrow can end after the reference's last use, before the lexical block ends.

answers.text: The last uses of `r1` and `r2` occur before `r3` is created, so the borrows do not overlap
`println!` converts `r1` and `r2` into owned copies of the `String`
A mutable reference may coexist with any number of active immutable references
`r3` is not considered a reference because it is used only to call a method

questions.explanation: The immutable borrows end after the last uses of `r1` and `r2`; a non-overlapping `&mut s` can then be created.

questions.text: Why is `fn dangle() -> &String { let s = String::from("hello"); &s }` rejected?

answers.text: `s` is dropped when the function ends, so the returned reference would become invalid
A `String` cannot be created inside a function
The function must return `usize`
References can only be returned from `main`

questions.explanation: The local `s` leaves scope and is freed, so a reference to it cannot be returned.

questions.text: What is a slice in Rust?

answers.text: A reference to a contiguous sequence of elements in a collection
An owned copy of the entire collection
Only an index marking the end of a string
A type available only for arrays

questions.explanation: A slice refers to a contiguous sequence of elements and is a kind of reference.

questions.text: Does a slice own its data?

answers.text: No; a slice is a reference and does not own the data
Yes, always
Only string slices own data
Only array slices own data

questions.explanation: The material explicitly says that a slice, as a kind of reference, does not have ownership.

questions.text: What problem exists in the version of `first_word` that returns only a `usize`?

answers.text: The index is detached from the state of the `String` and may become stale after the string changes
`usize` cannot be returned from a function
The index is always zero
A `String` cannot be cleared

String
str[]
&StringSlice

answers.text: A slice from index 0 up to but not including index 5
A slice containing only byte 5
A slice with indices 0 through 5 inclusive
A copy of the whole string

answers.text: &str
String
char

questions.text: Which statements about simultaneous mutable references are correct? Select all correct answers.

answers.text: Two active `&mut` references to the same data cannot exist at once
The restriction makes mutation controlled
The restriction helps prevent data races
There is no limit on simultaneous `&mut` references to the same data

questions.explanation: The material connects exclusivity of mutable references with preventing data races.

questions.text: Which conditions are required for a data race? Select all correct answers.

answers.text: Two or more pointers access the same data at the same time
At least one pointer is used to write the data
There is no mechanism synchronizing access
All participants only read immutable data

questions.explanation: A data race requires shared access, at least one writer, and no synchronization.

questions.text: Which approaches allow multiple mutable references to one value sequentially rather than simultaneously? Select all correct answers.

answers.text: Limit the first reference to a separate block
Create the second reference after the first reference's scope ends
Do not use the references at the same time
Create both before the block and use them together

questions.explanation: Non-overlapping scopes allow mutable references to be created sequentially.

questions.text: Which combinations of references to one value are permitted when their active scopes overlap? Select all correct answers.

answers.text: One mutable reference
Multiple immutable references
Any number of mutable and immutable references simultaneously
Two mutable references if both are used later

questions.explanation: The rule is either one mutable reference or any number of immutable references, but not both modes at the same time.

questions.text: Why does an active mutable reference conflict with an active immutable reference? Select all correct answers.

answers.text: A user of an immutable reference expects the data not to change unexpectedly
A mutable reference can change the value
The rule prevents overlapping reads and writes
Because an immutable reference automatically owns the data

questions.explanation: The material motivates the rule through predictable reads: data must not change beneath an active immutable reader.

questions.text: What follows from non-lexical lifetime rules for a sequence of several `&T` borrows followed by an `&mut T` borrow? Select all correct answers.

answers.text: Immutable borrows may end before the end of the block after their last use
An `&mut T` is allowed after all earlier immutable borrows have ended
The key requirement is that an active `&mut T` must not overlap active `&T` borrows of the same value
Every reference remains active until the closing brace regardless of its last use

questions.explanation: NLL can end a borrow after its last use; the rules prohibit overlapping conflicting borrows rather than requiring every borrow to last to the block end.

questions.text: Which statements about dangling references are correct? Select all correct answers.

answers.text: They may point to memory that has already been freed
The Rust compiler tries to prevent them
The data must not go out of scope before the reference to it
The `dangle` function in the material compiles successfully unchanged

questions.explanation: The `dangle` example specifically demonstrates a compilation error that prevents a dangling reference.

questions.text: A function creates a local `String`. How can it safely return that newly created string to the caller? Select all correct answers.

answers.text: Return the `String` by value
Move ownership of the string from the function to the caller
This avoids leaving a reference to a destroyed local value
Return an `&String` pointing to the local variable after the function ends

questions.explanation: Returning an owned `String` moves the value out. Returning a reference to a local `String` that will be destroyed is not allowed.

questions.text: Which borrowing rules apply to references in Rust? Select all correct answers.

answers.text: Either one mutable reference or any number of immutable references
All references must be valid
Mutable and immutable references to the same data can be freely mixed at the same time
Any number of dangling references are allowed as long as they are not dereferenced

questions.explanation: The section ends with two rules: exclusive write versus multiple readers, and validity of every reference.

questions.text: Why is storing only a numeric index into a `String` more fragile than storing an `&str` slice? Select all correct answers.

answers.text: A numeric index by itself does not borrow the source string
After the string is changed or cleared, the saved number may no longer describe the same logical data
From a plain `usize`, the compiler cannot tie use of the index to the validity of a particular string
A `usize` automatically prevents modification of the string from which it was once computed

questions.explanation: A plain index carries no borrowing relationship to the string. A slice is tied to the source data and is checked by the borrow checker.

The slice length
A relationship to the original data
An independent deep copy of the whole `String`

questions.text: What advantages does returning an `&str` have over returning a standalone index for part of a source string? Select all correct answers.

answers.text: The result directly refers to a range of the source data

The result type expresses a relationship between the found part and the source string
